utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Would the registrar please call the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Cross-examination is continuing with counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We are trying to be focused today really on the facts and we shall very briefly pass over the examinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to know whether all copies of the document that I mentioned yesterday were transmitted in the proper way, a document of Muslim party headquarters that I mentioned yesterday. Do we have enough copies for all parties or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Which one was it? The one --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It was the last one without numbering. I just -- because I have enough -- I have enough copies now, and maybe it's easy -- maybe it's better -- yes. I think that's the one, with the translation in English. So if necessary, we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Do you want it produced?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to have a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Just wait. The Prosecution, I hope you had a chat about the document. What's your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, I don't have -- I can understand the document can be marked, but what I was given yesterday, Your Honour, is a three-page document. It bears an ID number from another case, but it's apparently been faxed three times. I have two pages of an English translation and one page in B/C/S, and it's apparent that the English translation goes up through point 4, paragraph 4, and has a signature, while the B/C/S only has three paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So when you were discussing, you didn't compare what Mr. Pantelic is producing and what he gave you? You didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, I don't read B/C/S, but I didn't notice that until after I left court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry, my dear colleague, there is a 4 in the B/C/S version. I don't know. Maybe --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps I don't have that copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's the problem. So now, Your Honours, I have enough copies here. Maybe it was a problem with the stapling. So please, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can the usher assist, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This is six copies. Ms. Taylor, is it okay, six copies for all parties? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I would like the prosecuting counsel to describe the document he has just received so we see whether we have an identical document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I received a document consisting of three pages -- excuse me, four pages. The first two pages are in B/C/S and show at the very top line what I presume is a fax identification with a phone number. I don't think it's necessary to read it into the record. It was faxed at 7.47 a.m. on September 12th of this year. The English translation, the first few lines in English are: "SDA Party of Democratic Action, to SDA Srbinje, regarding the instructions from moving out from Srbinje."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is it only one page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry. The English is only one page. So I have four pages in total.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Mumba.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The last page on the -- is there a name at the bottom of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What's the name?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: "Secretary of SDA, Hasan Cengic."

utterances.speaker: MR. PANELIC
utterances.text: Cengic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Cengic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is that the same, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So now we have an identical document. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, I would have an objection to it being admitted for a lack of foundation, lack of authenticity. I don't know where it came from. But if counsel's simply marking it for identification, I don't know where it came from, but I understand he has the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, to speed up the things, this document is existing actually in Krnojelac case, Foca second case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We shall have an ID number. Then later on, when you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I just mentioned that to my colleagues, so they were able enough to check it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have an ID number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document, entitled Instructions From the Party of Democratic Action, shall be titled -- marked for identification ID2/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, could you tell us if you ever met in person -- personally, Mr. Hasan Cengic, the Secretary-General of Muslim SDA party?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Being an expert for Bosnian and Muslim topics, we can agree, can we not, that this Muslim party, among other members, also included Croat neighbours -- members and Serbian members of party?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very few. Very few members, yes, Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But assuming that they -- based on what you said on the previous occasions, that these members would be, by religion, by their religion, Christians?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recognise that I made that statement earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. Could you assume now?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So these Croatian and the Serbian members might be Muslim by origin or --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What's your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My question was that assuming that there were some members, Croat members and Serb members, within the SDS Muslim party. So my question is simple. What would be the religious background of these Croat and Serb members?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They may have been unbelievers, atheists. I can draw no conclusions about their religious --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And also Christians?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could be anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Catholic or Orthodox?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could be anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you inform us now, at the end of this document there is a -- there is a word which is at the end of the letter, Selam Aleykum. Being an expert for Muslim issue, could you tell us what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the document in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I would object to the characterisation of Dr. Donia as an expert for Muslim issues. He hasn't characterised himself that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Being an expert for Bosnia maybe, to be more precise, just tell us, what does it mean, Selam Aleykum? Because in your CV, I see that you are speaking also the other languages, including Serbian Croat. Although this is not maybe other language.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I won't speak either Turkish or Arabic, which would be the origins of this, but it is a term of greeting, "hello," "good-bye," that came into widespread use in the 1990s among some Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You mean Bosnian Muslims, to be more precise?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I indicated, in September 1993, the Bosnian Muslim leadership voted to change its name from Bosnian Muslim to Bosniak. So the answer is, in the period prior to roughly September 1993, one would refer to these people as Bosnian Muslims, thereafter as Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that, and I appreciate your explanations, but here within this Tribunal, we are operating with different notions and different words. It means Bosnian Muslims for this ethnic group, Bosnian Serbs for the other, and Bosnian Croats for the third. So it's just a matter of procedural issues, you know. So tell me, Mr. Donia, would it be correct to say that during the war in Bosnia, all three national parties undertook certain steps with regard to the armaments of their units, formations?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Including the SDS Muslim party?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the SDS was the Serbian party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, including the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Including the SDA. Would it be correct to say that the army wing of SDA party, Muslim party, called Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: An armed formation that was under the control of the SDA as -- I would characterise the Patriotic League that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And would it be correct to say that during the conflict in Bosnia, very many volunteers came outside of Bosnia to fight for various causes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by "very many"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thousands, let's say.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think a few thousand would be perhaps a better characterisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Including -- now we are focusing on the Muslim side in the conflict. It is -- I believe it's an indisputable fact that the Mujahedins, the extreme members of Muslim community, and I would say of factions within Muslim community, were also present in Bosnia as members the Bosnian Muslim army forces.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is there a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's a question.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear a question. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So in fact, could we agree upon the fact that the members of extreme part of Muslim community called Mujahedins were present at Bosnia under the control of Bosnian Muslim army? In some parts, of course.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's two parts to your question. Were they present? I would agree, they were present in numbers, as I've indicated, which could be characterised perhaps as a few thousand. I'm not in a position to render a judgement on whether they were under the control of any Bosnian formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Donia. Tell me, are you familiar with the fact that during the attack of these extreme Muslim members called Mujahedins, they used to yell -- they used to scream - sorry - to scream Selam Aleykum Allah Akbar? And I'm speaking specifically about the members of these army groups.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any direct knowledge of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me something about the other issue? You were a very frequent visitor of Sarajevo. When was the first time when you were in Sarajevo, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good. And at that time do you remember maybe what were the colour of the names of the street plates?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, they were - and some of them still are - dark blue with lettering on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good. And do you maybe remember some of the main streets' names? For example, could we say that certain streets at that time were named as, let's say, boulevard of JNA, or Tito, or Brotherhood and Unity, you know, in these Communist terms?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. All streets were named after some Communist hero or Partisan hero or organisation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good. Now, tell me, Mr. Donia, you claim that you visited also Sarajevo during the recent years - 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995 - I mean, after the 1990s, after the multiparty elections; yes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What is the colour now of the plates, of the street plates in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the course of my visits there, more and more of them have gone from that dark blue to a green.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that - I don't want to make any conclusions - that a green colour actually is the basic colour for Muslims on their flags, on their details, stuff like that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it's the party -- or the colour that the SDA prefers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no. In general terms, Mr. Donia, speaking about the Islam community in whole.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't speak to the entire Islamic community, but certainly the Muslim community and, say, from Saudi Arabia --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. It's enough for me. Another question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, I think the question is a simple one: Green is the basic colour of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And my answer is: I can only speak for that area that is from Saudi Arabia to the west. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: What's your answer for that, then?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours, but I'd just like to go to another question, because I really believe that we are wasting time here. So that was my -- that was my initial approach, to cut this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Donia, are you familiar about the names, the actual names of the streets now in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Comparing to the Communist-regime street names, could we agree upon the fact that the street names now in Sarajevo are labelled with Muslim origins, for example: Muslim heroes, Muslim writers, Muslim artists, Muslim heroes in the civil war, even Mujahedins, et cetera, et cetera, but all focused on Muslim names?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all. Not all, but many.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Many. Thank you. Now, Mr. Donia, yesterday you mentioned that you are a co-founder of the Donia Vakuf Foundation. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just -- it's not an important matter, but maybe it's -- it's maybe a word game. Do you know that in Bosnia there are two places called Gornji Vakuf and Donja Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So probably the idea when you have established your foundation was to be, let's say, more familiar with the local topics and names, and then combining your family name, you established the foundation Donia Vakuf, which sounds like Donia Vakuf. Is it true or -- I mean --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a pun, a bad pun, but it's a pun.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good. Thank you. So could we agree upon the fact that the process of reconciliation, interethnic reconciliation, interconfessional reconciliation in Bosnia, is a crucial one these days?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, could we agree upon the fact that due to the tragic war in Bosnia, still there are wounds between three communities, I mean wounds on them in their spirit, in the family life, in that these three communities are suffering a lot and, with the help of International Community, with the progressive elements in Bosnian society, trying to resolve these problems, to cure these wounds now?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good. Could we agree upon the fact that the Bosnian anthem is Beethoven's Ninth Symphony?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The anthem, you know, the official song of the state. Yes, anthem.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, anthem, hymn. I don't know what it is. I don't know what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we agree upon the fact that now official the flag of Bosnia-Herzegovina is a blue flag with the yellow -- one triangle and the stars?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good. So there is not any green --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- in this flag. So in the -- well, for your information, because I want to pose another question. Because the official anthem is, believe me, it's the Ninth Symphony, the Joy, the Ode to Joy of Beethoven. So could we agree upon the fact that the International Community and the progressive elements in Bosnia now are trying to be very sensitive among three ethnic communities not to give an advantage to one of them, and they are trying to balance, because this is a very sensitive time? Could you agree or not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good. But still, Mr. Donia, you being a humanist and a person very committed to the peoples of Bosnia, what was the reason for you not to establish a branch of your foundation, for example, in Bosnian Serb territory in Banja Luka, because -- or in Mostar, because these regions are also a part of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Or maybe you are thinking about that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My -- the Donia Vakuf Foundation is one stack of papers on my desk. It has no office, it has no location.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good. But tomorrow maybe you are --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it has very few funds.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, but -- well, I wish you all the best with your foundation, but probably tomorrow you may consider as a good idea to have your branch office in Sarajevo, Mostar, and Banja Luka, covering all territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would love to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Donia. So tell us: What was the reason to use the Muslim and Turkish notion of foundation which we yesterday discussed called Vakuf, a strictly Turkish and Muslim? Is it maybe a one-side approach when you established your foundation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Why you didn't, for example, say, "This is a foundation for all three communities in Bosnia. This is a Muslim, Croat, and Serb foundation," something like that? Tell me, what was your basic idea to name your foundation as the Vakuf Foundation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought it was a pun on "Donja Vakuf," the name of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Donia. I would like to introduce the documents. Actually, this is a translation of the Croat dictionary with this word, with this word "Vakuf," a translation in English too. Good, Mr. Donia. Just one small question. Tell me: I think that being a founder of such a foundation is an honourable thing. I mean, I would be proud if I would be a co-founder of one foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have an ID number, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- for the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This shall be marked for identification purposes as ID3/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask the Court a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I understand these documents are only being admitted for identification, but I presume counsel is going to use them in his examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The point here is that if all these documents that are being marked ID only and being objected to will be kept by the Registry. If, at a later stage, the parties don't agree as to the admission and they don't raise the point, that means the evidence on that will not be considered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's the position with such documents. So it's just that the witness is here, we can't hope to recall him, so we go through it. If at the end of the day it cannot be admitted, then that evidence will not be considered by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I just was -- my only concern was whether this was an official translation. But thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You can discuss that afterwards, because it's only marked for ID purposes. It may be not admitted later on, depending on what the Prosecution will say about it. We've already discussed the problem of translation, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm sure that Mr. Pantelic is aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I already mentioned -- yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much for this remark. And I would be very grateful, I would be very, very grateful if my learned colleagues from Prosecution would provide us a translation service. I would be so happy, because now we can -- in that situation we could resolve all this matter of whether it's official or not, because obviously members of Defence team are no expert of such .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just so we can establish the procedure, I think probably my colleague --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, my dear colleague. If you want to speak about the issue of interpretations, I would prefer to speak that after, because we have a witness here and we're in the middle of cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you can wait. The Trial Chamber has given counsel permission to address the Court, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Counsel indicated he'd ask the Prosecution to do the interpretation. I'm not sure what the practice of this team has been, but my understanding was that the counsel is to ask the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Translation Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: -- Translation Unit to provide it. The Prosecution itself cannot provide an official translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As I said, Your Honours, I would like to move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, tell me, would it be fair to say that in October of 1991, in Bosnia, the very serious tensions among and between three ethnic communities occurred and that all three ethnic communities tried to establish their own national goals, including, to some extent, to provoke a certain hatred on the other side or to arrange armament, et cetera, in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several questions, I think, you asked there. Could you ask one at a time so I could give you an answer, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, could you summarise your answer regarding these questions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you asked, in the first instance, if there were tensions between the national communities in October of 1991, and my response was yes -- or my response would be yes. October of 1991, there were already acute tensions between the national communities. The second part of the question that I heard was were these national communities as, let's say, spokesmen by their national parties engaged in arming. Yes. Were they engaged in a process of provocation, which was another part of your question. I think that is not so clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Donia. Would it be correct to say that the media took a very important role in this process of raising up tensions in -- well, a number of media, to be more precise, in Bosnian community?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Including Muslim media?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good. Mr. Donia, I would like --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, please, could you put this on the ELMO? I have also a translation, and I have enough -- enough copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: When you present a document, please describe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. Sorry, Madam President. That was my mistake. I am now introducing a document, the cover page of Muslim newspaper - I suppose it's weekly newspaper - published in October 1991. The name of this paper is Novi Vox, meaning New Voice or New Vox. So on the ELMO, we now see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the ID number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The ELMO is working.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document shall be marked for identification purposes ID/4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I take it the Prosecution is seeing it for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So at a later stage you will have your comments, after verifying it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So now, Mr. Donia --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: May I proceed? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Counsel may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We have on our displays cover page of Novi Vox. You are familiar with this newspaper, actually. You were there on many occasions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good. Thank you for your answer. The unofficial translation, as you see, Your Honours, and my dear colleagues from Prosecutor bench, says that the title of this cover page is, to the best of my knowledge, is "Handzar Division Ready." Is that correct, Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you agree with me that Handzar Divisija was a Muslim SS unit during the Second World War, under the command of German SS headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we agree upon the fact that this cover page of this Muslim -- Bosnian Muslim magazine might provoke, to some extent, a certain level of fear among the Serbian community? If you are a Serbian, for example, just to put the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before the question is answered, counsel for the Prosecution is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think it calls for the witness to make pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The objection is sustained. Do not ask questions to ask the witness to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Would you explain us, Mr. Donia, or try describe to describe the cut heads at the end of this -- at the bottom of this cover page, from left to right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see the one to the left. I understand you're representing these here to be Radovan Karadzic, Nikola Koljevic, Milosevic, and Seselj. I don't see those names on this document. They're reasonably poor caricatures of those four people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Donia, speaking about the events in the area of Samac, are you familiar with the fact that certain number of Croatian army units intervened in that region, crossing Sava River and commit -- and these Croatian units committed certain serious crimes against the Bosnian Serb population at that time in the neighbouring area of Samac?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the crimes were committed in -- or could we agree upon the fact that these crimes were committed in the region and in the villages of Sijekovac, Odzak, even Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I referred to that, I believe, in my paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, Mr. Donia, both of us have an agreement upon the fact, not interpretation but the simple fact that the certain numbers of amendments were adopted in 1990, in July 1990; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And that these amendments are related to the constitutional mechanism of the equality of nations and the mechanism of the protection of vital national interests; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we agree upon the fact that newly adopted Bosnia constitution, which is a part of NATO peace accord, I believe it's Annex 4, also provides even -- even more stringent provisions regarding the possibility of outvoting of one of the ethnic communities and the mechanism for preventing to -- for majority to outvote minority, and also the new Bosnian constitution in Dayton Peace Accord has a mechanism with a veto for this kind of decision which might affect the vital national interest in one of three communities in Bosnia? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to introduce the Official Gazette of Socialist Republic Bosnia and Herzegovina, published in 1990, consisting of amendments to the Constitution. Also, it's highlighted. All relevant parts are highlighted. Also, first part of constitution at that time in force in Bosnia, with the provisions of Article 1, 2, and 3, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have an ID number only pertaining to the highlighted parts, as counsel said.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The highlighted parts of this Gazette shall be marked for identification purposes ID5/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good. Mr. Donia, my next question would be: Can we agree upon the fact that in the process of scientific approach, historic approach to certain issues --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before you proceed, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Madam President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I notice that the highlighting is only in the other language. The English translation of the Official Gazette is not highlighted. Is the translation only pertaining to the highlighted parts?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct, Madam President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So speaking about the process of scientific approach to certain matter and issue for scientific research, could we agree, Mr. Donia, both of us, that to some extent, various angles of view and interpretation and process of taking something out of context of general picture might be characterised as a sort of manipulation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So, Mr. Donia, speaking about the famous memorandum of Serbian Academy of Arts - and you also mention this memorandum - could you agree with the following statement: "The sovereignty of the people, at the very foundations of modern civilisation, is the idea that political power is wasted in the people, that the sole legitimate political authority is the one which derives from the freely expressed will of the people and that, therefore, there are no moral or legal grounds for an elite by the will of God, by blood, religion, race, class, ideological credentials, historical merit, or any other grounds to arrogate to itself the right to speak, decide, or use force on behalf of a nation." Does this expression, does this thesis -- do you agree with this thesis?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I would like now to introduce this -- I know. I'm respecting the time of these Judge, and there are various points from this memorandum in order to illustrate this situation. My idea was to just take something out from context and then to have a characterisation. Thank you, Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the ID number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This memorandum shall be marked for identification purposes ID6/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good. Mr. Donia, would you agree with me, because you mentioned a poet --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, if you could.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: After you submit a document, give us a minute to read it through.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Pardon me. That's my mistake. Sorry, Your Honours. Excuse me. May I proceed, Your Honours? Just give me a sign, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, speaking about Njegos and his work, The Mountain Rat [sic] -- sorry, my bad English. "Mountain Wreath." Could we agree, both you and me, about the following thesis: "To write about Njegos at the present time is, of course, slightly hazardous. The fascist Balkan tragedy that is being played out with the aid of the powers of Western Europe and America has led to nationalistic feelings that have been seen to act adversely on the acceptance of the national culture of all parties. Thus there have been attacks on the works of Ivo Andric, who is a Nobel Prize winner in 1961, and also on Njegos. I am informed that some nitwit wrote article suggesting that Njegos wrote in favour of genocide. People have always been and, I fear, always will be thus, but perhaps one might quote the words of George Samson regarding Milton's "Paradise Lost," a poem does not become unreadable when its technology is no longer accepted." Would you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not fully. Not fully, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What document is that? Because we haven't -- is it within ID6?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. That's another document that I'm going to provide you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What you should be doing, before you read anything out of a document, you introduce it, you let us have it, let every party have it before you read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I appreciate. Thank you for your directions, Madam President. So this is a part of the book of the author Goy, "The Saber and the Song," Njegos, "The Mountain Wreath," published in Cambridge by one of the well-known Njegos - this is the last paragraph - expert for Njegos work. So I have these four copies here. Six, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This extract titled "The Saber and the Song" shall be marked for identification purposes ID7/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Donia, although you are not a constitutional lawyer, an expert for constitutional law, but speaking from your heart, from your soul, speaking from your personal point of view about certain protections and mechanisms in modern civilisation in the state with the rule of law, would it be correct to say that for important issues in one society in terms of constitutional law issues, at least a qualified a majority, at least two-thirds of votes for changes of borders or for changes of the structure of the state might be followed? That means -- my question is for you, having known all these issues and also knowing the situation in Bosnia, because you rely in your report on certain events in Bosnian parliament, so my question is: Would you agree with me, with the thesis that for the serious constitutional issues, for the serious national and vital national issues, the certain safeguards within the constitutional frameworks must be followed, as a person?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What was the last part of your question? Certain what?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Certain safeguards in the constitutional framework in order to prevent over-voting and, you know, to protect the vital interests of the nation must be followed.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Your Honours, I'm introducing two documents. First is chapter 4 of the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time in force, regarding the mechanism how and with which majority it can be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: When you say "at that time," what year? What year?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's year -- well, in 1991 and 1992 as well, prior to conflict, it was in force. This constitution was enacted in 1974, and then with the amendments that I just provided to you prior to my submissions, in 1990. So that's a whole issue. And also I would like to provide the constitutional provisions from the Bosnia and Herzegovina constitution that I mentioned yesterday with regard to the association of the municipalities and the constitutional framework for this. So two documents. Only a few, I think one or two, articles are highlighted, and then the English translation follows the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first document, with "Cooperation and Association of Municipalities" at the top shall be marked for identification purposes ID8/4, and the other document with "Change of the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina" at the top shall be marked for identification purposes ID9/4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, could we agree upon the fact that in October 1991 a memorandum about the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina was adopted by the majority of Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat delegates in the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we also be agreed upon the fact that by this act, the pattern of the qualified majority and also the mechanism for the protection of the interest of -- vital interest of one of three constitutive nations were not followed by this particular memorandum?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What is your position? Would you agree or not with the following approach? I'm now citing the book "The War in Bosnia-Herzegovina: Ethnic Conflict and International Interventions," written by Steven L. Burg and Paul S. Shoup. I suppose, Mr. Donia, that these names are familiar to you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honours. Yes. The usher, please. It's page 78, chapter 3, and the paragraph 1, 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So first of all, would you agree with me, Mr. Donia, that these two authors are well-distinguished American scholars with a very impressive work, especially in regard with the issue of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So now, this --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry. ID? Shall I wait for ID number or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, please. Can we have the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This extract from "The War in Bosnia-Herzegovina" shall be marked for identification purposes ID10/4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And Mr. Pantelic, before I forget, when discussing these documents which the Prosecution have yet to make a stand on, please make the book available to them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. By all means, Madam President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I don't want to challenge certain parts of your report with referring to the other parts of the other sources. I mean, it's the never-ending story. But just as a matter of fact, Mr. Donia, could we agree with the following interpretation: "The memorandum justified --" I believe it's the second paragraph: "The memorandum justified the actions of the parliament as a matter of constitutional principle. It asserted that the position in the memorandum," speaking about memorandum of sovereignty, "expressed the will of the majority of the Assembly and, as such, the political will of the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Consequently, they constitute an obligatory basis for the conduct of the state and political bodies of the republic. This seemed to contradict to the next point in the memorandum that the Assembly recognise simultaneously the right of the parliamentary minority to claim and realise every one of its legitimate interests - ethnic, cultural, economic, and social - provided this is achieved without the use of force and in a legal and democratic manner." Then the author says: "The rights of the minority does depend entirely on how 'legitimate interests were defined,'" et cetera, et cetera. Then I'm going to the second paragraph: "Changes in borders of Bosnia, the platform stated, could only be approached with a two-thirds vote in a popular referendum." And then we are coming to the expression: "While 'constitutional' in nature, the memorandum and the platform hardly reflect the kind of consensus necessary to make a constitution meaningful. Instead, they appear to reflect the efforts of one or two groups to impose their will on the third. In this respect, the Bosnian Muslim leadership was simply following the practice that had taken hold in Yugoslavia since 1988, majorities using constitutional reform as a weapon to impose their own political agendas on minorities," et cetera, et cetera. So could you agree, both of you, that this assumption and this approach would be correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: An objection to Mr. Donia commenting, because part of this section that was read out deals with constitutional issues. He's testified he's not a constitutional law expert. I don't know if the authors of this document are either, but I'd like to cross-examine them about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The objection is sustained, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam President. Let me rephrase this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, being an expert for Bosnia and Herzegovina issue and also well informed about the events in Bosnian parliament in the time of 1991, speaking from a position of historian and speaking to some extent from position of a layperson with regard to the issues, constitutional issues, would you agree with me that this chapter reflects, on realistic and objective manner, the situation in Bosnia at October 1991?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not wholly, no, I would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Donia. Tell me, by the way, why you didn't mention in your CV that you are a co-founder of Donia Vakuf Foundation that we spoke of earlier? What is the reason? I mean, I would be proud to put in my CV such thing.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you saw the resources that the foundation has, you'd realise that it's practically pocket change. It's not worth mentioning. It's not a significant amount of money. It's not a significant institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I believe that we are not speaking about money. I'm speaking about your efforts as a historian, as a scientific person, to work for the welfare of all three ethnic communities in Bosnia, and especially you are committed to all these cases here. Why not simply put this fact in your CV? That was my question, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, Counsel. It's not correct to say that the witness is committed to all these cases here. It is the decision of the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Madam President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- to choose experts for their cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So it's not the choice of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I absolutely concur with your position. Thank you so much. Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good. Mr. Donia, let's finish this. Mr. Donia --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Usher, I have some documents here. These are six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What are these documents we are receiving?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Madam President, I would like to present to the -- as a matter of fact, as a matter of clarification, I would like to present to the witness certain provisions of various constitutions with regard to the mechanism of preventing the, you know, important interests in the states, as well as the national interests. These are the, by chance, Constitution of Zambia, then Constitution of Singapore, and Constitution of Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So would you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Are these constitutions current?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Excerpts, yes. Highlights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no. What I'm asking is: Are these the constitutions which are valid today?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So can you describe each one, for which country, so we know what we are discussing?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's right. I just want to -- although Mr. Donia is not an expert for these issues, but still, my question is -- you know, the spirit of law --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no. You haven't described the documents yet, so we don't know what these things are.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Donia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no. Not Mr. Donia. Address the Trial Chamber. Tell the Trial Chamber. You have so many documents. "The first one I would like to discuss is so-and-so," dated whatever. Then we have the number. And the second, you know, before you ask the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. Madam President, the first document is the excerpt from the Constitution of Zambia preamble, speaking about the -- well, speaking about the protection of nations, and also speaking about the mechanism and the way how certain important constitutional issues should be followed, by which principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the number, please, from the registry?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The extract from the Constitution of Singapore shall be marked for identification purposes ID11/4. The extract from the Constitution of Canada shall be marked for identification purposes ID12/4, and the extract from the Constitution of Zambia shall be marked for identification purposes ID13/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I address the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask the Trial Chamber to ask counsel what the relevance of these three documents, which apparently are going to take at least some of the Court's time, are. I don't think the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, you are taking the words out of my mouth, because I wanted them described first and then we deal with that. So counsel may as well answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Madam President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Particularly that the witness is not a constitutional expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. We know that, but still we are making a certain comparison between the fact that existed in Bosnia in terms of constitutional law in 1991, and the expert is actually covering this period of events in October 1991. And then my question to him would be not focused on his constitutional law knowledge, but rather the principle of fairness, the principle of his personal feelings to certain provisions, not more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The other point is that the witness is seeing these constitutional provisions for the first time in the witness box, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not trying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So how does --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If you will allow me, I will just pose the question: Mr. Donia, could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no. You see, Mr. Pantelic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: "Could you agree with me with the following expression," nothing more, and now we are finishing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. The witness hasn't had an opportunity to study this. He doesn't even know the background political policies, constitutional theories of these countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: At least not to the knowledge of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I am focusing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So he cannot answer anything on these documents, Mr. Pantelic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Then he's free to say, "No, I'm not familiar."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no. The Court cannot allow a question which is basically unfair to a witness to be asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's part of our duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. But my position was, Madam President, just to give an impression about the constitutional mechanism, because this witness is relying on certain mechanism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no. His expertise is on the country which he has discussed. He didn't discuss Singapore, Zambia, Canada, unless you show us the particular paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will show you, Madam President. That's my intention. I would like to submit to the witness a certain -- as I already submitted Constitution of Bosnia at that time, and this witness is speaking -- I don't know, actually -- I don't have the paragraph here, but on the first version of his report, which is, yes, paragraph 93 in his report, that to -- very extensively about constitutional matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: If I may assist you a little bit there. Now, generally in constitutional provisions around the world, it is well known that legislative changes can be made by a simple majority. But insofar as constitutions are concerned, it is also generally known, or well known, that these vital -- there are vital safeguards for the nation which can only be amended or done away with a two-thirds majority. Perhaps you want to pose that question to the witness as part of a general --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Your Honour. That was my -- exactly my intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: So that you don't need these documents then. Just ask him this. Perhaps he will be able to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour, for my assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So we are speaking in your report about the process of referendum, about the process of plebiscite, about the sovereignty of the nation, and also to some extent about the domestic, Bosnian domestic mechanism of protection of the rights of ethnic communities in Bosnia. And now my question would be: Could you agree, Mr. Donia, that -- for example, you said -- I'm don't remember, but correct me if I'm wrong. You said that there is no Muslim nation as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, you haven't posed the question that you started off on and which I rephrased for you. Would you like to ask that question or would you like to abandon it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Donia. I would like to pose you the following question: Could you agree with me with the fact that based on the well-developed constitutional systems in the world, a two-thirds majority for sovereignty -- for voting for sovereignty or for changes of borders or in order to protect the vital interests of the nation should be followed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't -- that's a constitutional question. I just don't know that much about other constitutional systems. I can't answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Donia. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it that's the last counsel, because I was told four counsel. That's the last counsel. Thank you. The Prosecution, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I hope to be very brief. I would like to ask the witness questions about one document that was put to him by counsel for Mr. Blagoje Simic, and that was the report to the General Assembly from the Special Rapporteur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Has it got a number?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I believe it's ID --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The registry will announce the number for us so that we all know which document to look at.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This number has been marked for identification purposes as ID2/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Counsel. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, in your knowledge of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia, was it common for the various parties who had been involved in war crimes to attempt to hide those crimes from the International Community?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Referring to the report that counsel showed you, the first counsel to cross-examine you, regarding the trip of -- I've been trying to avoid pronouncing his name, so I've been called him "the Special Rapporteur," but I believe it's Mr. Mazowiecki. Turning to paragraph number 28, is it not correct that the Special Rapporteur reported to the Security Council that the Special Rapporteur has had only limited access to prisons and other places of detention in Serbian-controlled Bosnia? Is that true? Is that what he reported?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Turning now to the conclusions of the report in paragraph 134, did not the Special Rapporteur conclude that: "Between the first and second missions of the Special Rapporteur in August and October 1992, ethnic cleansing has continued and in some regions intensified. Arbitrary executions, terrorist attacks against homes and places of worship, and the taking of hostages continue, primarily in Bosnia and Herzegovina but also in the UN-protected areas. The victims are primarily Muslim and Croatian civilians." Did he report that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And I'd like you to comment on the next conclusion of the Special Rapporteur. It's correct that he concluded that: "The continuation of ethnic cleansing is a deliberate effort to create a fait accompli, in flagrant disregard of international commitments entered into by those who carry out and benefit from ethnic cleansing." Did he report that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And how does this conclusion of the Special Rapporteur fit into the point made in your report about creating facts on the ground by ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it basically states that same reality, perhaps at a time in advance of the international negotiations that made it reality, but it was a reference to ethnic cleansing as a strategy to secure maximum territorial advantage for the party engaged in ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. To speed things up, we're happy to stipulate to this report that there was ethnic cleansing. It's just that the point is, it didn't happen, according to this report, in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. Counsel is reading the report itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: But we're going to stipulate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: He's not giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: We were just going to stipulate, to save time, that the report is accurate and that we agree that there was ethnic cleansing, just not in Bosanski Samac. Just to kind of speed things on. That's all I offer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm very familiar with strategies. Counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I've finished my redirect examination. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Donia, for assisting the Tribunal with your evidence. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It's just the right time to go back to our outstanding matters and our decisions on the outstanding motions, and then the parties can raise other matters before we go for our break or before we call the next witness. The decision on the Prosecution motion to have one additional witness, that is Roko Jelavic, added to its witness list, filed on 7 September; and the response of Milan Simic dated 10 September; and the same response the three other defendants joined in orally. The decision of the Chamber is as follows: Pursuant to Rule 73 bis, "After the commencement of a trial, the Prosecutor may, if he so wishes ..." up to the end of the Rule. It does give the Prosecutor the liberty to vary the list of witnesses or to include another witness they had originally left. The Trial Chamber notes that the Prosecution withdrew Roko Jelavic from its witness lists of its own volition. The Trial Chamber is satisfied that this witness was withdrawn from the list on account of his health and not because his testimony would be considered repetitive. The Trial Chamber is satisfied that his testimony is relevant and does not constitute new charges. The presentation of his evidence will not prejudice the Defence or any defendant who have already got the witness statement and who were previously able to prepare for this particular witness who was withdrawn from the list on 6 July. So the parties have enough time. The Prosecution motion is granted. The next motion was filed -- it was a joint Defence motion in limine regarding legal conclusions. This was by all the four accused, filed on 10 September. This motion is misconceived, in the view of the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber finds that it's not necessary to ask the Prosecution to respond, hence its decision. Drawing legal conclusions based on the interpretation of facts presented by witnesses forms part of the Trial Chamber's duties in the performance of its task. A witness or indeed counsel, therefore, cannot be allowed to make legal conclusions. The motion is dismissed. The next one was the accused Blagoje Simic motion for determination on the issue whether Bosnia and Herzegovina was a state in terms of international law prior to 22nd May, 1992. This motion was filed on 27th August this year, and the Prosecution responded on 31st August. The Defence motion may be understood as merely intending to raise the issue of status of Bosnia and Herzegovina before 22nd May, 1992. At this stage of the proceedings, recognising that this is matter for trial, as one of the paragraphs in the Defence motion mentions and that they are not seeking an immediate decision. The issue raised in the motion is a matter to be determined at trial after both parties have presented their evidence. It is therefore not necessary for the Trial Chamber to make a ruling at this stage. However, the Trial Chamber takes judicial notice of the fact that both parties -- of the fact agreed by both parties that Bosnia and Herzegovina was admitted as a member of the United Nations on the 22nd May, 1992. I wish to remind the parties that the Pre-Trial Chamber also took judicial notice of the other facts in relation to the same issue on 25th March, 1999, if you check the records of the proceedings of this case, at pre-trial stage. Bosnia and Herzegovina proclaimed its independence on 6th March, 1992, and the second fact that was taken judicial notice of it was that the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state was recognised by the European Community on 6th April, 1992, and by the United States on the 7th of April, 1992. Besides that, the other matters will be decided after the trial is over, when both parties have adduced their evidence. We may as well use this time for any other matters or any other oral motions that the parties may have. I'll ask the Prosecution. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Thank you. If Your Honours please, the only matter that I wanted to raise on the issue of motions was the question of the admission of the telephone interviews, but that has already been decided upon, and so therefore, before I say anything further about that, I must ascertain whether the Chamber is prepared to hear from me on that issue, a decision already having been made. In other words, do you regard yourselves being functus officio and the matter is closed, or do you wish to hear from me in respect of the further matters that I did wish to put to the Chamber on that issue? If you take the view that the matter is now closed and beyond argument, I won't proceed any further. If you wish to hear from me, however, I've got a few brief submissions to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Unless you are discussing matters concerning our decision which do not raise in issue the decision itself. MR. DI FAZIO: In issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber's decision itself that the three excerpts cannot be admitted into evidence. If your address is on the motion but not raising -- not objecting to the decision of the Trial Chamber. But if it's a question of -- I don't know whether in such a matter you can have additional evidence or anything like that. I doubt it. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. That's essentially what it is. It was just some factual background to one of the issues that the Trial Chamber raised, which was the awareness of the defendants being interviewed of the indictment. You asked me some questions about that, about that matter, and I wanted to respond, but in the meantime, I received a copy of the decision, and that's all that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you can say it. Let's have it on the record. Perhaps we can respond right away. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. If Your Honours, please, there were, in fact, substantial moves made to inform all of the defendants in this case of the existence of the indictment. The indictment was confirmed by Judge Vohrah on the 21st of July, 1995, and you'll find this information in a report on measures taken by the Prosecutor for the personal service of the indictment and warrants of arrest, and that report was put in on the 28th of May, 1997. I believe it forms part of the court record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: And was signed by, I believe, the counsel then acting in the case, Ms. Nancy Paterson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: She reported that arrest warrants had not been executed and that the Prosecutor had taken reasonable steps to provide the defendants with information about the existence by seeking publication -- existence of the indictment by seeking publication of newspaper advertisements announcing the indictment. On the 19th of October, 1995, the Registrar sent the original arrest warrants to the Prime Minister of the Bosnian Serb administration in Pale, Republika Srpska. That was a gentleman named Mr. Dusan Kostic. And also to a gentleman named Danilo Dusan. He was at the bureau of Republika Srpska. So the government authorities, in effect, in the Republika Srpska were informed. At the time Lugar, or Slobodan Miljkovic, was also included on the indictment. He apparently had knowledge of the fact that he was being charged, because he provided an interview in a Serbian newspaper called Telegraph on the 19th of December, 1995, in which he was quoted as saying that he had received a booklet from Belgrade entitled "Rules of Procedure and Evidence" and "Rules Governing Detention," and that he said that this indicated that the Hague got its information from Belgrade and that in fact, "I am being tried in Belgrade." So he was obviously aware that he was in some sort of trouble, so to speak, with the -- in respect of indictments issued against him. On the 23rd of January, 1996, advertisements regarding the indictments were sent by the Registrar of this -- of the ICTY to the Charge d'Affaires of the embassy of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in The Hague and again to Mr. Dusan Kostic, Prime Minister of the Bosnian Serb administration in Pale in Republika Srpska. On the -- later that -- on the 7th of October, although -- that's not relevant. I'll withdraw that. And then of course, on the documents itself, you can see, if you read through the documents, that there was obviously a considerable awareness on the part of the defendants of the predicament in which they faced, namely, the issuance of the indictments and the charges against them. And indeed, if you go through the recorded -- the transcript of the recorded telephone conversations, you will see that they have an awareness of the fact that the ICTY investigators were interested in them, awareness of rights, and presence of counsel, and you can see that throughout the -- throughout the three telephone interviews. On the 26th of April, 1996, the first telephone conversation, telephone interview occur. If you read it, you will see at page 1 that it was really a telephone conversation initiated by Mr. Tadic, Mr. Miroslav Tadic. You'll see that again at page 3. And at page 4, he offered to answer questions. In respect of his, Mr. Tadic's, awareness of rights, he was advised of his rights on page 3, and he stated that he was speaking voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but counsel, before you proceed with Mr. Tadic, let's say, is there any evidence that the indictment was served on him? MR. DI FAZIO: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before that first interview or even the second or even the third interview? MR. DI FAZIO: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is there any evidence -- as we put in our decision, that we were not satisfied that he was fully aware of -- MR. DI FAZIO: If that is regarded -- if the fact of delivery of the indictment into their hands is regarded as the crucial factor, then I can't assist the Tribunal any further. If that's the view that you take, that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's the view of the Trial Chamber, because the rules on service of the indictment and interrogation of an indicted person are clear. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The moment the accused spoke to whoever on the Prosecution side and they knew that he was a person who had been indicted, they should have followed the steps of making sure the indictment is served and it is understood by the suspects. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, if that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because that was the basis of our decision. We were not satisfied that they understood what the indictment was all about in the absence of service and that they realised that they were facing war crimes. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We are not satisfied. So nothing more -- MR. DI FAZIO: As the Chamber pleases, I'll abandon that application to re-open the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So our decision stands. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. The other issue that I wanted to raise is a general one regarding the documents in this case for the future. In 1999, there was an order made admitting the evidence, the documentary evidence in this case, into evidence. That followed upon a Prosecution submission which had been filed on the 10th of February, 1999. It was entitled, Prosecutor's Request for Admission of Documentary Evidence, and it had attached to it an annex, which I have attached, too, myself, and it indicated that the Prosecutor sought the admission of a number of documents. Now, the documents on that annex, although not corresponding entirely with the documents that form the 65 ter list of exhibits, was substantially the same, and it included many of the -- what the Prosecution regards as its crucial documents, Variant A and B documents and so on. They're almost completely the same, apart from the addition of a few documents that occurred in later years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: And in the course of the submission of the motion, rather, Ms. Nancy Paterson said: "Virtually all of the attached documents are either official documents provided by governmental agencies, the records of the controlling Serb political party, or documents obtained from the relevant authorities at the Banja Luka Military Court. The majority of the attached documents were either provided to the Prosecution by one or more Defence counsel or were given to the Office of the Prosecutor by governmental authorities in Bosanski Samac, Odzak, Orasje, and Banja Luka." And then contended that issues relating to the authenticity and reliability should not preclude their admission at this stage, and submitted that the relevance and probative value of the documents is apparent from the face of the documents. Remember, at this stage they were coming up for trial, I believe, and subsequent events meant that this trial that we're now engaged in was postponed for various reasons. An order followed that motion, on the 19th of March, 1999, signed by His Honour Judge May presiding, and it said: "The Prosecution request for admission shall be granted and the documents listed in the annex shall be admitted subject to the right of the defence to object to the admission of any particular item at the time it is presented in evidence." I'm not entirely sure what that means, but it seems to say yes, they're admitted, but you can object to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll discuss that, I think, after our break. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because it is after 11.00 now. Then we'll give the Defence the right of response, as usual, so we can decide firmly what the status of these orders and the documents is now that the trial has opened. We will take our break now and resume the proceedings at 11.30 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We were discussing the issue of documents or any other matters. The Prosecution. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. If Your Honours please. To get to the point, my concern is to try and identify the documents that are going to be objected to. That's why I've raised this issue of their having been admitted subject to objection back in 1999. And we've seen that there was some confusion when the Variant A and B document was sought to be introduced into evidence. That caused a flurry of activity on the part of the Prosecution with gathering evidence, authenticating the document, and so on, and that's an exercise that I'd like to keep to a minimum if I could. So that could be avoided if there is a direction to the Defence that they tell the Prosecution which particular documents out of that list of 112-odd documents that are on our 65 ter list, which of those documents they object to. We will then be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because I thought that was dealt with at the pre-trial stage. They were informed if they have any objections and all that. When you discussed behind the scenes with them, they should have indicated that. I thought that stage would have been reached already. MR. DI FAZIO: I thought it had. I might -- perhaps I was wrong in that, particularly given the existence of this motion. So that's what I'd like to do so that I can say we can ascertain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
